slides.title: Reading a Python expression
slides.body:
An expression is code that produces a value. In 7 + 2, the inputs are 7 and 2; the operator + tells Python to add them.

A statement is an instruction. total = 7 + 2 calculates 9, then gives it the name total. print(total) displays the stored value.

Read each symbol before running. Code is what you type; output is what Python displays. Do not type the word “Output”.

slides.title: Reading powers signs and remainders
slides.body:
2 ** 3 means 2 × 2 × 2. It does not mean 2 × 3. The left value is the base; the right value is the exponent.

A leading minus makes a number negative: -7. Floor division rounds the quotient down: -7 / 2 is -3.5, so -7 // 2 is -4.

% is remainder, not percentage. To turn 75% into a fraction, calculate 75 / 100. Do not divide by zero.

slides.title: Which operation happens first
slides.body:
Parentheses group a calculation: do (2 + 3) before multiplying it by 4.

Powers come before multiplication and division. Multiplication, /, // and % come before addition and subtraction. Equal-level * and / run left to right.

Use parentheses when the intended grouping might be unclear. For a negative base, write (-2) ** 2. This gives 4; -(2 ** 2) gives -4.

slides.title: Assigning and updating a named value
slides.body:
count = 2 gives the name count the value 2. = means assignment; it does not ask whether two values are equal.

count = count + 1 first reads the old value 2, calculates 3, then assigns 3 back to count.

After the update, print(count) displays 3. Re-running only the update cell changes count again; restart and run from the beginning for the shown result.

slides.title: Numbers text and conversion
slides.body:
7 is an integer. 7.0 is a decimal-valued float. "7" is text because it is inside quotes. Both single and double quotes can enclose text.

"7" + "2" joins text into "72". To add those digits as numbers, convert each first: int("7") + int("2") gives 9.

int converts valid integer text; float converts valid decimal text. str turns a value into text. print displays a value; type reports its Python type.
slides.notes:

CONNECT

EXPLAIN
7 is an integer. 7.0 is a decimal-valued float. "7" is text because it is inside quotes. Both single and double quotes can enclose text.

"7" + "2" joins text into "72". To add those digits as numbers, convert each first: int("7") + int("2") gives 9.

int converts valid integer text; float converts valid decimal text. str turns a value into text. print displays a value; type reports its Python type.

slides.title: Arithmetic that needs care
slides.body:
Parentheses run first: (2 + 4) / 2 is 3.0. Without them, division runs before addition: 2 + 4 / 2 is 4.0.

/ gives a quotient. // rounds that quotient down: 7 // 2 is 3 and -7 // 2 is -4.

Many decimal fractions are approximate in a computer. A tolerance is an allowed difference, for example 0.01 m when checking two calculated lengths.

slides.title: None means there is no result value

A function returns None explicitly with return None. A function also returns None if it reaches its end without a return value.

A caller must handle None before trying arithmetic with the result. The next example returns it for division by zero.

slides.title: Read every part of a for header

in connects the current-item name to that collection. The colon begins the loop body. Four spaces mark each instruction that repeats.

reading is a name we choose; it is assigned the next item automatically. It is not the same name as readings. After the last item, execution leaves the loop.

slides.title: Updating a counter inside a loop
slides.body:
A counter records how many times an event happens. Set count = 0 before the loop, then count = count + 1 inside it.

count += 1 is a shorter spelling for that numeric update. Similarly, total += reading means total = total + reading.

The initial value belongs outside the loop. Resetting count to zero inside every iteration loses the earlier count.

slides.title: A while loop checks before each repetition
slides.body:
while count < 3: tests the condition before entering its indented block. True enters the block; False skips it and continues after the loop.

At the end of the body, return to the condition and test again. Unlike for, while does not automatically move to the next list item.

Something must make the condition become False, or the loop may continue indefinitely. In our example, count increases on every iteration.

slides.title: Tuples and unpacking
slides.body:
A tuple stores items in order. point = (2, 3) stores two coordinates; point[0] is 2. You cannot reassign point[0].

x, y = point gives the first item to x and the second to y. This is unpacking; the number of names must match the number of items.

A tuple prevents replacing its positions. It does not freeze the contents of a mutable object stored inside it.

slides.title: A bar chart and a histogram count different things
slides.body:
A bar chart has named groups. bar(["A", "B"], [13, 16]) makes one bar for each supplied group value.

A histogram divides a numeric range into intervals called bins. hist(readings, bins=2) counts readings in two intervals.

With [12, 14, 13, 18], the intervals run from 12 to 15 and 15 to 18. Counts are 3 and 1; the final interval includes the last endpoint.

A list comprehension builds a new list using an expression for each visited item. [value * 2 for value in readings] doubles each reading.

Its first part says what to store; its for part says which items supply value. [2, 4, 6] becomes [4, 8, 12].

This compact spelling is optional. Use the expanded loop already taught when that is easier to explain.

slides.title: A fitted line is a numerical rule
slides.body:
For these invented observations, target = 2 × input + 10 matches all four points. 2 is the slope; 10 is the intercept, the value at input zero.

A prediction error is the difference between a prediction and the measured answer. A vertical gap in the picture shows that error.

Fitting chooses the slope and intercept to minimise summed squared errors. Squaring means multiplying an error by itself; a small training error still needs an unseen-data check.

A prediction error is the difference between a prediction and the measured answer. A vertical gap in the picture shows that error.

Fitting chooses the slope and intercept to minimise summed squared errors. Squaring means multiplying an error by itself; a small training error still needs an unseen-data check.

slides.title: Read the pipeline tools before combining them
slides.body:
np.nan is NumPy’s missing-number marker. SimpleImputer(strategy="median") creates a tool that will learn each column’s median from training data.

make_pipeline(imputer, model) joins preparation to prediction in that order. pipeline.fit first learns and applies the imputer, then fits the model.

pipeline.predict applies the already learned imputer to new inputs before predicting. It does not recalculate medians from the new inputs.

slides.title: R² compares against a mean prediction
slides.body:

1 means perfect predictions on those observations. 0 matches that mean-prediction reference; a negative score can be worse.

Use the same evaluation observations and report the specified error metric with its units. Constant targets need special handling; this score alone does not prove usefulness.

slides.title: Accuracy can hide missed warnings
slides.body:
Accuracy = number of correct labels / number of labels. It counts correct warnings and correct non-warnings together.

If 90 of 100 cases need no warning, predicting no warning every time gives 90% accuracy. It detects none of the 10 real warnings: recall is 0.

Always inspect the actual/predicted counts and relevant costs before calling a classifier useful.

slides.body:

SD describes spread around the mean in the score’s units. The next illustration uses this same population convention; it is not a confidence interval.

slides.title: Read the physical example across programmes
slides.body:
Current I is the flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A). Resistance R opposes that flow, measured in ohms.

Power P is energy transferred per second, measured in watts (W). Resistive heating follows P = I²R in this example.

I² means I × I. With I = 2 A and R = 3 ohms, P = 2 × 2 × 3 = 12 W. This relationship motivates a feature; evaluation still tests whether it helps.

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
train = [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 2], [4, 4], [5, 3]]
y = [3, 5, 5, 8, 8]
validation = [[2, 2], [3, 3]]
truth = [4, 6]
def with_interaction(rows):
    result = []
    for a, b in rows:
        result.append([a, b, a * b])
    return result
base = LinearRegression()
base.fit(train, y)
extended = LinearRegression()
extended.fit(with_interaction(train), y)
base_predictions = base.predict(validation)
base_error = mean_absolute_error(truth, base_predictions)

validation_features = with_interaction(validation)
extended_predictions = extended.predict(validation_features)
error = mean_absolute_error(truth, extended_predictions)
print(round(error, 6))

slides.title: Scaling changes units of comparison
slides.body:
A distance calculation can be dominated by a feature with larger numerical values. Scaling puts feature values on a chosen numerical scale.

One example is (value - training_min) / (training_max - training_min). With training limits 10 and 30, value 20 becomes 10 / 20 = 0.5.

Use the same learned limits for new observations. A zero training range needs a defined handling rule. New values outside the training range may scale outside 0 to 1.

Name the positive class first. Actual is what happened; predicted is the model decision. Precision asks how many predicted positives were right. Recall asks how many actual positives were found.

slides.title: Reading powers signs and remainders
slides.body:
2 ** 3 means 2 × 2 × 2. It does not mean 2 × 3. The left value is the base; the right value is the exponent.

A leading minus makes a number negative: -7. Floor division rounds the quotient down: -7 / 2 is -3.5, so -7 // 2 is -4.

% is remainder, not percentage. To turn 75% into a fraction, calculate 75 / 100. Do not divide by zero.

slides.title: Which operation happens first
slides.body:
Parentheses group a calculation: do (2 + 3) before multiplying it by 4.

Powers come before multiplication and division. Multiplication, /, // and % come before addition and subtraction. Equal-level * and / run left to right.

Use parentheses when the intended grouping might be unclear. For a negative base, write (-2) ** 2. This gives 4; -(2 ** 2) gives -4.

slides.title: A comparison produces a Boolean value
slides.body:
A comparison asks a yes/no question about values. Its Python result is True or False, written with capital first letters and no quotes.

30 >= 30 asks “Is 30 at least 30?” The answer is True. 28 >= 30 gives False.

True and False have type bool. "False" is text, not the Boolean value False. Conditions use Boolean results to choose what happens next.

slides.title: A condition and an if block
slides.body:
A condition is the question tested by an if statement. if reading >= 30: checks whether reading is at least 30.

The colon ends the header. The next line starts with four spaces; those spaces place it inside the block controlled by if.

If the condition is True, run the block. If it is False, skip it. The next line without those four spaces is outside the block and runs afterwards.

slides.title: else gives the other path
slides.body:
else means “otherwise”. It has a colon but no extra condition. Align else with its matching if.

The if block runs when its condition is True. The else block runs when that same condition is False. Only one of these blocks runs.

Both branch bodies are indented by four spaces. Returning to the left margin ends the whole decision.

slides.title: Why a zero check comes first
slides.body:
Python evaluates and from left to right. When the first Boolean comparison is False, it does not need to evaluate the second.

For a simple zero guard, use if denominator == 0: before the division and return or handle that case explicitly.

We will demonstrate that guard inside a function after learning how def and return work.

A named constant stores a value kept fixed in the calculation. Uppercase names such as G are a convention, not a Python restriction.

slides.title: A while loop checks before each repetition
slides.body:
while count < 3: tests the condition before entering its indented block. True enters the block; False skips it and continues after the loop.

At the end of the body, return to the condition and test again. Unlike for, while does not automatically move to the next list item.

Something must make the condition become False, or the loop may continue indefinitely. In our example, count increases on every iteration.

slides.title: Find the median by sorting the readings
slides.body:
The median is a middle value after ordering the numbers from smallest to largest. In [2, 4, 30], the middle item is 4.

With an even number of readings, average the two middle values. [20, 22, 24, 80] has middle values 22 and 24, so the median is 23.

None is missing information in our list, not a number to sort. Collect only recorded values before calculating this median.

slides.title: A bar chart and a histogram count different things
slides.body:
A bar chart has named groups. bar(["A", "B"], [13, 16]) makes one bar for each supplied group value.

A histogram divides a numeric range into intervals called bins. hist(readings, bins=2) counts readings in two intervals.

With [12, 14, 13, 18], the intervals run from 12 to 15 and 15 to 18. Counts are 3 and 1; the final interval includes the last endpoint.

A list comprehension builds a new list using an expression for each visited item. [value * 2 for value in readings] doubles each reading.

Its first part says what to store; its for part says which items supply value. [2, 4, 6] becomes [4, 8, 12].

This compact spelling is optional. Use the expanded loop already taught when that is easier to explain.

slides.title: A fitted line is a numerical rule
slides.body:
For these invented observations, target = 2 × input + 10 matches all four points. 2 is the slope; 10 is the intercept, the value at input zero.

A prediction error is the difference between a prediction and the measured answer. A vertical gap in the picture shows that error.

Fitting chooses the slope and intercept to minimise summed squared errors. Squaring means multiplying an error by itself; a small training error still needs an unseen-data check.

slides.title: A matrix is a rectangular table of numbers
slides.body:
A matrix has rows and columns. For modelling, one row is one observation and each column is one input feature.

[[1, 20], [2, 22]] has two rows and two columns. The outer list contains rows; each inner list contains that row’s features.

X is a conventional name for this input table. y holds one known target per row. These names have no special power in Python.

slides.title: R² compares against a mean prediction
slides.body:
R² compares squared errors with predicting the mean of the evaluated targets. It is a score, not “percentage accuracy”.

1 means perfect predictions on those observations. 0 matches that mean-prediction reference; a negative score can be worse.

Use the same evaluation observations and report the specified error metric with its units. Constant targets need special handling; this score alone does not prove usefulness.

slides.title: Accuracy can hide missed warnings
slides.body:
Accuracy = number of correct labels / number of labels. It counts correct warnings and correct non-warnings together.

If 90 of 100 cases need no warning, predicting no warning every time gives 90% accuracy. It detects none of the 10 real warnings: recall is 0.

Always inspect the actual/predicted counts and relevant costs before calling a classifier useful.

slides.title: What standard deviation tells us
slides.body:
Scores 3, 4 and 5 have mean 4. Their deviations are -1, 0 and 1.

For these three fold scores, population SD = sqrt((1 + 0 + 1) / 3), about 0.82.

SD describes spread around the mean in the score’s units. The next illustration uses this same population convention; it is not a confidence interval.

slides.title: Read the physical example across programmes
slides.body:
Current I is the flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A). Resistance R opposes that flow, measured in ohms.

Power P is energy transferred per second, measured in watts (W). Resistive heating follows P = I²R in this example.

I² means I × I. With I = 2 A and R = 3 ohms, P = 2 × 2 × 3 = 12 W. This relationship motivates a feature; evaluation still tests whether it helps.

Each row contains two inputs. for a, b in rows: assigns them to a and b. [a, b, a * b] builds a new row with their product as a third input.

slides.practice_code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
train = [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 2], [4, 4], [5, 3]]
y = [3, 5, 5, 8, 8]
validation = [[2, 2], [3, 3]]
truth = [4, 6]
def with_interaction(rows):
    result = []
    for a, b in rows:
        result.append([a, b, a * b])
    return result
base = LinearRegression()
base.fit(train, y)
extended = LinearRegression()
extended.fit(with_interaction(train), y)
base_predictions = base.predict(validation)
base_error = mean_absolute_error(truth, base_predictions)
print(round(base_error, 6))
validation_features = with_interaction(validation)
extended_predictions = extended.predict(validation_features)
error = mean_absolute_error(truth, extended_predictions)
print(round(error, 6))

    for a, b in rows:
        result.append([a, b, a * b])
    return result
base = LinearRegression().fit(train, y)
extended = LinearRegression().fit(with_interaction(train), y)
base_predictions = base.predict(validation)
base_error = mean_absolute_error(truth, base_predictions)
print(round(base_error, 6))
validation_features = with_interaction(validation)
extended_predictions = extended.predict(validation_features)
error = mean_absolute_error(truth, extended_predictions)
print(round(error, 6))

slides.title: Scaling changes units of comparison
slides.body:
A distance calculation can be dominated by a feature with larger numerical values. Scaling puts feature values on a chosen numerical scale.

One example is (value - training_min) / (training_max - training_min). With training limits 10 and 30, value 20 becomes 10 / 20 = 0.5.

Use the same learned limits for new observations. A zero training range needs a defined handling rule. New values outside the training range may scale outside 0 to 1.

slides.title: Pass a function as the sorting key
slides.body:
sorted returns a new list in order. In sorted(eligible, key=rank), rank is the function itself, passed without calling it.

sorted calls rank(item) for each candidate and compares the returned tuples. Writing rank() here would call it immediately without its required input.

The original eligible list is unchanged. Check len(ordered) before using ordered[0], because an empty list has no first position.

slides.title: Reading powers signs and remainders
slides.body:
2 ** 3 means 2 × 2 × 2. It does not mean 2 × 3. The left value is the base; the right value is the exponent.

A leading minus makes a number negative: -7. Floor division rounds the quotient down: -7 / 2 is -3.5, so -7 // 2 is -4.

% is remainder, not percentage. To turn 75% into a fraction, calculate 75 / 100. Do not divide by zero.

slides.body:

Powers come before multiplication and division. Multiplication, /, // and % come before addition and subtraction. Equal-level * and / run left to right.

Use parentheses when the intended grouping might be unclear. For a negative base, write (-2) ** 2. This gives 4; -(2 ** 2) gives -4.

int converts valid integer text; float converts valid decimal text. str turns a value into text. print displays a value; type reports its Python type.

slides.body:

/ gives a quotient. // rounds that quotient down: 7 // 2 is 3 and -7 // 2 is -4.

Many decimal fractions are approximate in a computer. A tolerance is an allowed difference, for example 0.01 m when checking two calculated lengths.

A condition is the question tested by an if statement. if reading >= 30: checks whether reading is at least 30.

The colon ends the header. The next line starts with four spaces; those spaces place it inside the block controlled by if.

If the condition is True, run the block. If it is False, skip it. The next line without those four spaces is outside the block and runs afterwards.

slides.title: Updating a counter inside a loop

A counter records how many times an event happens. Set count = 0 before the loop, then count = count + 1 inside it.

The initial value belongs outside the loop. Resetting count to zero inside every iteration loses the earlier count.

slides.title: A while loop checks before each repetition
slides.body:
while count < 3: tests the condition before entering its indented block. True enters the block; False skips it and continues after the loop.

At the end of the body, return to the condition and test again. Unlike for, while does not automatically move to the next list item.

Something must make the condition become False, or the loop may continue indefinitely. In our example, count increases on every iteration.

slides.title: A set remembers distinct items
slides.body:
A set is useful when the question is “Have we seen this ID?” It keeps one instance of each distinct item.

seen = set() creates an empty set. seen.add("A") adds an item. "A" in seen asks whether it is present.

Do not use a set when position or repeated readings matter. Sets cannot be indexed. {} creates an empty dictionary, not an empty set.

open("file.csv", newline="") opens a text file for reading. Use the actual supplied filename, including its .csv extension.

slides.title: Read a list comprehension after the full loop
slides.body:
A list comprehension builds a new list using an expression for each visited item. [value * 2 for value in readings] doubles each reading.

Its first part says what to store; its for part says which items supply value. [2, 4, 6] becomes [4, 8, 12].

This compact spelling is optional. Use the expanded loop already taught when that is easier to explain.

slides.title: R² compares against a mean prediction
slides.body:
R² compares squared errors with predicting the mean of the evaluated targets. It is a score, not “percentage accuracy”.

1 means perfect predictions on those observations. 0 matches that mean-prediction reference; a negative score can be worse.

Use the same evaluation observations and report the specified error metric with its units. Constant targets need special handling; this score alone does not prove usefulness.

EXPLAIN
Read the code in this order:
for truth, guess in zip(actual, predicted):
    if truth == 1 and guess == 1:
        tp += 1
    elif truth == 0 and guess == 0:
        tn += 1
    elif truth == 0 and guess == 1:
        fp += 1
    else:
        fn += 1

for takes the next item. The indented block repeats.

if tests a condition. The chosen indented block runs.

zip pairs items at matching positions in these equal-length lists.

Continue the SAME cell; keep indentation. Run after all parts are entered.

LECTURER CUE
Start every counter at zero before the loop. == compares labels. and means both comparisons must be true. elif checks another condition only when earlier ones were false.

Complete practice code:
tp = tn = fp = fn = 0
for truth, guess in zip(actual, predicted):
    if truth == 1 and guess == 1:
        tp += 1
    elif truth == 0 and guess == 0:
        tn += 1
    elif truth == 0 and guess == 1:
        fp += 1
    else:
        fn += 1
print(tp, tn, fp, fn)

slides.title: Accuracy can hide missed warnings
slides.body:
Accuracy = number of correct labels / number of labels. It counts correct warnings and correct non-warnings together.

If 90 of 100 cases need no warning, predicting no warning every time gives 90% accuracy. It detects none of the 10 real warnings: recall is 0.

Always inspect the actual/predicted counts and relevant costs before calling a classifier useful.

slides.title: What standard deviation tells us
slides.body:
Scores 3, 4 and 5 have mean 4. Their deviations are -1, 0 and 1.

For these three fold scores, population SD = sqrt((1 + 0 + 1) / 3), about 0.82.

SD describes spread around the mean in the score’s units. The next illustration uses this same population convention; it is not a confidence interval.

slides.title: Read the physical example across programmes
slides.body:
Current I is the flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A). Resistance R opposes that flow, measured in ohms.

Power P is energy transferred per second, measured in watts (W). Resistive heating follows P = I²R in this example.

I² means I × I. With I = 2 A and R = 3 ohms, P = 2 × 2 × 3 = 12 W. This relationship motivates a feature; evaluation still tests whether it helps.

from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error

validation = [[2, 2], [3, 3]]

    for a, b in rows:

slides.title: Scaling changes units of comparison
slides.body:
A distance calculation can be dominated by a feature with larger numerical values. Scaling puts feature values on a chosen numerical scale.

One example is (value - training_min) / (training_max - training_min). With training limits 10 and 30, value 20 becomes 10 / 20 = 0.5.

Use the same learned limits for new observations. A zero training range needs a defined handling rule. New values outside the training range may scale outside 0 to 1.
